title: The concept of layers
starter: A parcel goes in a box, the box goes in a sack, the sack goes in a van. What happens if the van is replaced by a train? Why does that not affect the parcel?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Why layers?
facts: Networking is a complex job, so it's divided into smaller, simpler tasks called layers.
Each layer has a defined responsibility.
Each layer provides a service to the layer above it.
stations.challenge: Why is it easier to solve a big problem in layers?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Networking is a complex job, so it's divided into smaller, simpler tasks called layers.
Also credit: Each layer has a defined responsibility.

questions.q: Why is networking divided into layers?
questions.a: To split a complex task into smaller, simpler tasks that work together

questions.q: What does each layer do for the layer above it?

stations.name: The parcel model
facts: A parcel goes in a box, the box goes in a sack, the sack goes in a van.
Swap the van for a train and the parcel inside doesn't change at all.
Each stage only has to deal with the stage next to it.
stations.challenge: Describe the four stages of sending a parcel, and say which one could be swapped without affecting the others.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A parcel goes in a box, the box goes in a sack, the sack goes in a van.
Also credit: Swap the van for a train and the parcel inside doesn't change at all.

questions.q: You change from Wi-Fi to an Ethernet cable. What else has to change?
questions.a: Nothing else: only the bottom layer changes

questions.q: In the parcel analogy, what does swapping the van for a train show?
questions.a: One layer can change without changing the others

stations.name: Advantages of layering
facts: Easier to develop and troubleshoot: you can work on one layer at a time.
Layers can be changed or upgraded independently.
Different companies can make products for different layers that still work together.
stations.challenge: State three advantages of layering a complex task like networking.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Easier to develop and troubleshoot: you can work on one layer at a time.
Also credit: Layers can be changed or upgraded independently.

questions.q: Which are advantages of layering protocols? Select all that apply.
questions.a: A layer can be changed without affecting the others; Problems can be traced to one layer; Different companies can make parts that work together

questions.q: A network technician is troubleshooting. Why do layers help?
questions.a: They can test one layer at a time to find where the problem is

stations.name: The four layers
facts: Application: the programs you use, e.g. HTTP, SMTP, FTP.
Transport: TCP makes sure data arrives reliably.
Internet: IP routes packets.  Link: the physical connection, e.g. Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
stations.challenge: Which layer does your web browser work in?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Application: the programs you use, e.g. HTTP, SMTP, FTP.
Also credit: Transport: TCP makes sure data arrives reliably.

questions.q: Put the four layers in order, from top (closest to the user) to bottom.
Which layer sends data over the actual cable or radio signal?

stations.name: Sending an email
facts: Your email app uses SMTP (application layer).
TCP makes sure it all arrives (transport layer).
IP routes it to the mail server (internet layer), over Wi-Fi (link layer).
stations.challenge: Show the jigsaw for sending an HTML email with no encryption over Wi-Fi to a mail server.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Your email app uses SMTP (application layer).
Also credit: TCP makes sure it all arrives (transport layer).

questions.q: Match each layer to the protocol used when sending an email over Wi-Fi.
questions.a: Application → SMTP; Transport → TCP; Internet → IP; Link → Wi-Fi

stations.name: Layers in action
facts: Loading a web page: HTTP (or HTTPS), then TCP, then IP, then Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
Each layer adds its own information, like putting a letter in an envelope.
The receiver unwraps the layers in reverse.
stations.challenge: Describe the layers used when you load a web page over an Ethernet cable.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Loading a web page: HTTP (or HTTPS), then TCP, then IP, then Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
Also credit: Each layer adds its own information, like putting a letter in an envelope.

questions.q: Which protocol would be in the application layer when loading a web page?
Which layer would change if you moved from a school PC on a cable to a laptop on Wi-Fi?

final.name: Final challenge: build the stack

questions.q: Which layer does each protocol or technology belong to?
questions.a: HTTP = Application; FTP = Application; SMTP = Application; IMAP = Application; TCP = Transport; IP = Internet; Ethernet = Link; Wi-Fi = Link

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Give three benefits of dividing networking into layers.
points: Networking is a complex job, so it's divided into smaller, simpler tasks called layers.
Layers can be changed or upgraded independently.
Different companies can make products for different layers that still work together.
The receiver unwraps the layers in reverse.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Explain how layering makes it possible to change from Wi-Fi to a cable without changing any software.
points: Swap the van for a train and the parcel inside doesn't change at all.
Transport: TCP makes sure data arrives reliably.
Internet: IP routes packets.  Link: the physical connection, e.g. Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
TCP makes sure it all arrives (transport layer).
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
